title: LinkedList internal working — doubly linked nodes, head/tail, use cases
shortTitle: LinkedList internal working — doubly linked nodes, head/tail, use cases

s1_definition.profdef: LinkedList is a **doubly-linked list** where each element is stored in a `Node` object: `Node { E item; Node<E> next; Node<E> prev; }`. The list maintains `first` (head) and `last` (tail) pointers. Adding/removing at head or tail: O(1) — just update 2-3 pointers. Random access `get(index)`: O(n) — must traverse from head or tail (optimized: if index < size/2, traverse from head; else from tail). LinkedList also implements `Deque` — usable as a double-ended queue. Memory: ~24 bytes per node (object header + item + next + prev) vs ArrayList's ~4 bytes per element reference.
s1_definition.analogy: LinkedList is a chain of STICKY NOTES. Each note says: "My data is X. Previous note is at location P. Next note is at location N." Adding a note at the front: stick a new note, point it to the old first note. O(1) — one operation. Finding note #500: start from note #1, follow the chain → 499 hops. O(n). Memory: each note has 3 fields (data + prev + next) — 6x more than just storing the data.
s1_definition.oneliner: Doubly-linked nodes (item + prev + next). O(1) addFirst/addLast/removeFirst/removeLast. O(n) get(index). Implements both List and Deque. 6x more memory than ArrayList.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** LinkedList is a **doubly-linked list** where each element is stored in a `Node` object: `Node { E item; Node<E> next; Node<E> prev; }`. The list maintains `first` (head) and `last` (tail) pointers. Adding/removing at head or tail: O(1) — just update 2-3 pointers. Random access `get(index)`: O(n) — must traverse from head or tail (optimized: if index < size/2, traverse from head; else from tail). LinkedList also implements `Deque` — usable as a double-ended queue. Memory: ~24 bytes per node (object header + item + next + prev) vs ArrayList's ~4 bytes per element reference.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** LinkedList is a chain of STICKY NOTES. Each note says: "My data is X. Previous note is at location P. Next note is at location N." Adding a note at the front: stick a new note, point it to the old first note. O(1) — one operation. Finding note #500: start from note #1, follow the chain → 499 hops. O(n). Memory: each note has 3 fields (data + prev + next) — 6x more than just storing the data.

**One line to remember:** Doubly-linked nodes (item + prev + next). O(1) addFirst/addLast/removeFirst/removeLast. O(n) get(index). Implements both List and Deque. 6x more memory than ArrayList.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The transaction undo/redo stack needed fast add/remove at BOTH ends.** Using ArrayList: `add(0, txn)` was O(n) — shifted all elements for every undo push. Fix: LinkedList as Deque — `addFirst()` for undo push (O(1)), `addLast()` for redo push (O(1)), `removeFirst()`/`removeLast()` for pop. Note: in modern Java, `ArrayDeque` is preferred even for this — but LinkedList works when you also need `ListIterator` access.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a sequence of transactions added to a `LinkedList` built from doubly linked nodes.

**Step 1.** Each `add` creates a new node holding the transaction and links it after the current tail, updating the tail pointer.

**Step 2.** Each node keeps both a `prev` and `next` reference, so the list can be walked forward from head or backward from tail.

**Step 3.** A `get(index)` must walk node by node from the nearer end to reach Rajesh's entry, which is why random access is O(n) while add and remove at the ends are O(1).
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ LinkedList INTERNAL STRUCTURE ═══

  first → [prev:null | item:A | next:→] ⇄ [prev:← | item:B | next:→] ⇄ [prev:← | item:C | next:null] ← last

  addFirst("Z"):
    new Node(null, "Z", first)  → update first pointer → O(1)!

  addLast("D"):
    new Node(last, "D", null)   → update last pointer → O(1)!

  get(1):
    first → next → item:B      → O(n) traversal!

  ═══ OPTIMIZATION: traverse from closer end ═══
  get(index):
    if index < size/2 → traverse from FIRST (head)
    else              → traverse from LAST (tail)
    Saves half the traversal!

  ═══ USE CASES ═══
  ✅ Deque (addFirst/addLast/removeFirst/removeLast)
  ✅ ListIterator insert/remove during traversal
  ❌ Random access by index (O(n) — use ArrayList!)
  ❌ Memory-constrained (6-10x more than ArrayList)
  ⚠️ ArrayDeque is usually better even for Deque use!
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   Transaction Queue (LinkedList as Deque)       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   addFirst                               addLast
      │                                      │
      ▼                                      ▼
  first ─► [Txn A] ⇄ [Txn B] ⇄ [Txn C] ◄─ last
   O(1)      doubly-linked nodes          O(1)
      ▲                                      ▲
   removeFirst (process FIFO)            removeLast
   get(index) → O(n) traversal (avoid)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
LinkedList stores elements in doubly-linked `Node` objects — each with item, prev, and next references. It maintains `first` (head) and `last` (tail) pointers. addFirst/addLast/removeFirst/removeLast are O(1) — just pointer updates. get(index) is O(n) — must traverse from head or tail (optimization: starts from the closer end). Also implements Deque interface — usable as a double-ended queue or stack.

LinkedList's true advantage: O(1) insert/remove AT the current position during ListIterator traversal — no element shifting like ArrayList. Memory overhead: ~40 bytes per node (object header + 3 references) vs ArrayList's ~8 bytes per element — 5x more memory. In modern Java: ArrayDeque outperforms LinkedList even for Deque operations (contiguous array = cache-friendly). Use LinkedList only when you need ListIterator-based insertion during traversal. For all other cases: ArrayList (random access) or ArrayDeque (queue/stack).
